parties:

full_judgment:
Syed Refaat Ahmed, J: This Rule Nisi was issued on 2-5-2011 calling upon the Respondents to show cause as to why they should not be directed to evict the trespassers from the case land measuring 5 (five) kathas of Plot No. 10 (ten), Road No. 1/A of Gulshan Residential Area, Police Station-Gulshan, Dhaka ("said property") and hand-over the vacant possession of the same to the petitioner in accordance with law and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 7. This is all the more surprising given that pursuant to the petitioner's Application of 15-4-2009. RAJUK on 29-6-2009 decided to hold an inquiry as to the petitioner's dispossession from the said property on 6-7-2009. The inquiry report produced recorded the fact that the said property was locked up with no one residing there and that in that case necessary steps could be taken to launch an eviction drive. 

 9. There is yet another dimension to this case that needs to be recorded here. The petitioner's case plays out against the backdrop of previous dealings in the said property that have come to bear upon her possessory and occupancy rights therein. This history of the claims and counter claims to the said property was only brought on record by the petitioner on 31.7.2016 through the second Supplementary Affidavit filed on her behalf. 

 10. The first date of note is 26-7-1964 when 32.85 acres of land of Mouza Bhola, PS Tejgaon, Dhaka (then Dacca) was ordered to be acquired by the then Additional Deputy Commissioner, Dacca in LA Case No. 10763-64 for extension of Gulshan Model Town. It is on 23-12-1964 that 31.34 acres land in the said Mouza including CS Plot No. 457 owned by one Mr Abdur Rahim was similarly ordered to be acquired with immediate effect, also under LA Case No. 10/63-64. Thirteen years later an order was passed on 31-3-1977 by the Joint Secretary of Ministry of Works regarding derequisition of 32.85 acres of land in LA Case No. 10/63-64. However, on 10-9-1977 a Final Requisition Order was passed by the Joint Secretary of Ministry of Works reviewing the Order dated 31-3-1977 regarding derequisition of 32.85 acres of land in LA Case No. 10/63-64. Being aggrieved by such Final Requisition Order one Mr Khademul Islam filed Writ Petition No. 835 of 1977 in respect of the scheme of acquisition of 32.85 acres of land in LA Case No. 10/63-64. The Rule was made absolute in Writ Petition No. 835 of 1977 on 12-7-1979, thereby, effectively upholding the order of derequisition of 31-3-1977. 

 12. From RAJUK's pleadings in this case it is evident that its account begins here as the initial requiring body. Having in that capacity devised the RAJUK Layout Plan, it allotted to Dr. M Rafiquzzaman the said property on 5-12-1989 which allotment can be termed as a direct consequence of the 1964 acquisition process. 

 14. A development of note as brought forth in the petitioner's second Supplementary Affidavit of 31-7-2016 occurred at this juncture. That is, on 8-2-1999 the Ministry of Land issued a notice directing the District Commissioner, Dhaka to take necessary steps to cancel the proceedings of LA Case No. 10/63-64 pursuant to the judgment dated 12-7-1979 in Writ Petition No. 835 of 1977. While parallel to these developments by the end of 1999 the petitioner, Mrs Naina Islam had already acquired a firm and entrenched title to the said property as above noted through a deed registered in her favour. 

 15. Pursuant to the Land Ministry's Order of 8-2-1999 a gazette of derequisitioned properties, including that of Mr Abdur Rahim, having been published on 11-11-1999 there was another development of note evident in a Review Petition being No. 13 of 1999 arising out of Writ Petition No. 835 of 1977 being rejected on 22-11-1999 by the Court. Drawing on parallel timelines related to this case, it is noted that soon after the said property was mutated in the petitioner's name in Mutation Case No. 111 of 2000 on 27-1-2000 the Appellate Division at the other hand dismissed on 31-7-2001 the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal being 122 of 2000 arising out of Review Petition No. 13 of 1999 and Writ Petition No. 835 of 1977. Accordingly, this gave rise to the situation where on the one hand the petitioner Mrs. Naina Islam was paying taxes and rates on the said property from 2000 to 2016, conflicting and potentially rival rights and interests were being created concerning the said property by forces unleashed through the judgment in Writ Petition No. 835 of 1977. 

 17. It is against this backdrop that Mr Abdur Rahim executed "saf kabala" in favour of the Added Respondent No. 8, Mr Abdus Salam Mazumder, termed by the petitioner to be the trespasser in this case, in relation to the sale of 16 and 2 Katha of land on 25-10-2004 and 1-11-2004 respectively. In the following period Mr Abdus Salam Mazumder applied for electricity and gas connections from the relevant utility service providers but having failed to acquire a clearance certificate from RAJUK filed Writ Petition No. 8679 of 2005. The High Court Division on 4-12-2005 having directed RAJUK to dispose of Mr Mazumder's application for a Clearance Certificate, the said Clearance Certificate was eventually issued by RAJUK on 2-10-2007. 

 21. It is pertinent to note at the outset that RAJUK has appeared in this case acknowledging the petitioner to be its actual lessee and also admitting that it has acted on the petitioner's application by taking steps to evict Mr Abdus Salam Mazumder, the trespasser, who has been added as the added Respondent No. 8 by virtue of this Court's Order dated 16-7-2017. A copy of that Order being duly served upon him as per our later Order of 21-11-2017, Mr Mazumder has not contested the Rule. For its part, despite the acknowledgment and admission as noted above, RAJUK claims nevertheless that this Writ Petition is not maintainable. 

 22. With RAJUK's unexplained volte face about evicting Mr Mazumder in mind, the petitioner, Mrs. Naina Islam puts forward the central thesis of her case. She asserts that given that RAJUK is the allotter of the said property under whose supervision the petitioner enjoys the rights of the ultimate lease holder, RAJUK by that reason is under an obligation to protect her right to property guaranteed under article 42 of the Constitution. By extension, according to the petitioner, RAJUK is also under a duty to recover the property of the petitioner, restore possession to her and, thereby, secure to her the protection of the law as enshrined in article 31 of the Constitution. 

 23. The Respondent Nos. 2 and 3 being RAJUK and its Chairman respectively are represented in these proceedings by their learned Advocate, Mr Md Imam Hasan. By filing an Affidavit-in-Opposition the said Respondents preliminarily assert that this Writ Petition is not maintainable. This stance predicated on their understanding that they have been divested of all responsibility regarding overseeing and protecting possessory and occupancy rights regarding the said property as early as on 23-12-1989 when the said plot was handed over to the original allottee, Dr. M. Rafiquzzaman. It is specifically submitted in that light that it remains the sole duty of the occupant-lessee in possession of the said property, i.e., someone in the position of the petitioner, Mrs Naina Islam to herself secure all rights incidental upon such possession and that in any case a matter of dispossession as this is to be agitated in a proper legal forum other one of judicial review as this. The Respondents have, however, not taken care to specify what other forum(s) may indeed be available to the petitioner in the circumstances. Having said that, the Affidavit-in-Opposition nevertheless reads to this Court as an attestation of all facts asserted by the petitioner as to her chain of title to the said property and the acquisition of such title through a permission of transfer from the original allottee granted by RAJUK itself. In other words, this Court notes at the outset, RAJUK asserts the petitioner's sole and exclusive right to control the said property and to exclude others therefrom. 

 25. It is to be noted here that the Affidavit-in-Opposition is wholly silent on the history of the said property involving LA Case No. 10/63-64 and its aftermath as has been extensively recorded above. 

 26. In presenting the petitioner's case, the learned Advocate Mr Ajmalul Hossain submits at the outset that despite several oral representations from the petitioner, RAJUK has persistently declined to disclose any reason for a sudden change of mind in evicting trespassers from the said property. Even after receiving a Notice Demanding Justice RAJUK is shown not to have taken any effective measures for eviction and handing over the vacant possession of the said property to the petitioner. 

 33. Given the above circumstances it can be said that the remedy as set out in section 9 of the Specific Relief Act is not alternatively an equally efficacious remedy for the petitioner and, therefore, the Writ is maintainable. Whether the remedy available is equally efficacious or not is usually determined by the court by examining the facts and circumstances of each case. Relevantly, in Inland Navigation Co. vs Income Tax Officer reported in 19 DLR 87 (Para 16) the High Court Division entertained a writ petition even where the petitioner had an alternative option to file an appeal against the rectified order of assessment of income tax but failed to do so upon a misconception of the law. Therefore, even if the petitioner in this case was under a misconception of law in not filing a suit for recovery of possession, she should not be barred from pursuing this Writ Petition since such misconception was contributed by RAJUK by acting upon the petitioner's application and promising the petitioner to evict the trespasser. 

 37. In the case of Ram Chandra Chatterjee vs Pramatha Nath Chatterjee reported in IC Vol. LXII! 758 it has been held that, "The landlord's undertaking for enjoyment by the tenant is implied from the relationship of landlord and tenant. [Transfer of Property Act, section 108 (c) Budd Scott vs Daniel (2), Markham vs Pagett (1)) and the undertaking would include the protection of the tenant from disturbance by the strangers claiming by title paramount." A similar view was taken in Syed Mukhtar Ahmad vs Rani Sunder Koer reported in CWN Vol. XVII Page 960 observing that, 

 40. Accordingly, in Cab Express (BD) Ltd vs Commissioner of Customs reported in 9 BLC 398 (Para 17 & 18) it has been observed that, "So it appears that the doctrine of promissory estoppel operates when one of the parties in reliance of the promise made by the other party acts to his detriment and in such case the other party should not be allowed to go back from his promise as the same would cause injustice on the party relying upon the said promise." A similar view was taken in Asaf Khan vs Court of Settlement reported in 8 BLC 1. 

 43. We note that section 108(A)(b) states that the lessor at the request of the lessee shall put him in the possession of the leased property and section 108(A)(c) states that the lessor shall ensure peaceful possession of the lessee over the leased property. In the instant case, the petitioner after being dispossessed by the Respondent No. 8 filed an application before RAJUK for eviction of the Respondent No.8 and to put her into the possession over the leased property. RAJUK after receiving the application internally discussed the issue, sought legal advice from its legal counsel and directed the petitioner to deposit Taka 70,000 and after receiving such direction from RAJUK the petitioner deposited Taka 70,000 to RAJUK. Thereafter, RAJUK initiated proceedings for eviction of the Respondent No. 8 from the leased property, but suddenly backed off from such eviction proceedings without assigning any reasons. As RAJUK by its own action has promised the petitioner to evict the Respondent No. 8 from the leased property and to put her into the possession of the leased property, we find that it is now bound by such promise by operation of the Doctrine of Promissory Estoppel. 

 45. Upon a consideration of the above, it is evident that the said property along with other properties were acquired on 23-12-1964 government for RAJUK (then DIT) under LA Case No. 10/63-64. After a considerable lapse of time, upon application of some aggrieved persons an order of derequisition was passed in the said LA Case on 31-3-1977 only to be revised on 10-9-1977 by the Final Requisition Order. Writ Petition No. 835 of 1977 was filed against the Final Requisition Order and by a resultant judgment of 12-7-1979 the High Court Division effectively restored the derequisition order of 31-3-1977. That led the Ministry of Land on 8-2-1999 to issue a notice directing the District Commissioner, Dhaka to cancel the proceedings of LA Case No. 10/63-64 and subsequently the Official Gazette Notification in evidence of such derequisition was issued on 11-11-1999. Subsequent challenges mounted against the judgment in Writ Petition No. 835 of 1977 in the form of Review Petition No. 13 of 1999, a CPLA arising out of the RevieW Petition both proved to be futile in upholding the validity of the Final Requisition Order of 10-9-1977. The Respondent No. 8, Mr Abdus Salam Mazumder consequentially had secured the Registered Deeds of 25-10-2004 and 1-11-2004 and obtained a Clearance Certificate from RAJUK on 2-10-2007 in circumstances recorded hereinabove. The said Registered Deeds were executed as the direct consequence of the Gazette Notification dated 11-11-1999 for derequisition of the said property. 

 46. It was now the turn for the derequisition order of 11-11-1999 to face a constitutional challenge from RAJUK in the form of Writ Petition No.5198 of 2003 along with several Writ Petitions filed against the same by others. After hearing the Writ Petitions, the High Court Division predicated on the rationes decidendi of a catenae of cases reported in 44 DLR (AD) 260, 3 MLR (AD) 91, 52 DLR 125, 52 DLR (AD) 176, 9 MLR (AD) 151, 46 DLR 205 and 50 DLR (AD) /I and made the Rule absolute by a Judgment and Order dated 15-11-2007 as found that given the provision of law and the decisions as referred to the entire purported derequisition exercise effected through memos and notifications issued by the Ministry of Land are illegal, mala fide and made without lawful authority and, therefore, shorn of any legal effect. In setting aside the Gazette Notification of 11-11-1999, that Court further ordered that, 

 48. That being the case, we find that the purported execution of the Registered Deeds and the issuance of the Clearance Certificate neither create any legal right in favour of the Respondent No.8 nor provide any excuses for RAJUK not to comply with its earlier promise to evict the Respondent No.8 from the leased property and restore the petitioner's possession of the same. 

 49. Upon a consideration further of the facts and grounds on issues of both maintainability as well as the issue of the conflicting rights of parties stemming from LA Case No. 10 of 1963-64 and going through the various twists and turns concerning derequisition and the rights that were created subsequently leading to the judgment in particular in Writ Petition No. 5198 of 2003, we are inclined to find merit in the Application and substance in the Rule issued. 

 50. The petitioner being led down the garden path by RAJUK and left high and dry abruptly, it is consequentially incumbent upon RAJUK to revive the stalled process of eviction of the trespasser from the case/leased property within the period of 6(six) weeks from the date of receipt of a certified copy of this Judgment and Order. It shall thereafter be incumbent upon RAJUK as lessor to ensure the Petitioner lessee's full possession and enjoyment of the said property and to facilitate the completion of all matters outstanding pertaining to the said property to the benefit of the Petitioner lessee.
